subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on AQA Business finance (sources of finance, cash flow, break-even, profit and ratios), then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain an AQA GCSE Business finance idea for GCSE Business simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Internal and external sources of finance
Short-term and long-term and the suitability of sources of finance
The importance of cash and cash flow forecasts
Interpreting a cash flow forecast and the difference between cash and profit
Revenue, costs, profit and loss and the break-even level of output
Break-even output, margin of safety and break-even charts
Average rate of return on investment
Purpose and components of financial statements
Gross profit margin and net profit margin

questions.lo: Internal and external sources of finance
questions.q: Which of the following is an INTERNAL source of finance?
questions.explain: Retained profit is generated inside the business, so it is an internal source. Bank loans, grants and trade credit all come from outside the business, so they are external sources.

questions.lo: Internal and external sources of finance
questions.q: Selling unwanted machinery to raise money is an example of:
options: An internal source of finance (selling assets)
questions.explain: Selling off assets the business already owns raises cash from within the business, so it is an internal source. Mortgages and share issues bring money in from outside.

questions.lo: Short-term and long-term and the suitability of sources of finance
questions.q: A business needs to cover a short-term gap when a large bill is due before customers have paid. Which source of finance is MOST suitable?
questions.explain: An overdraft is a flexible short-term source ideal for bridging a temporary cash shortfall. A mortgage, share issue or long-term loan are long-term sources, unsuitable and costly for a brief timing gap.

questions.lo: Short-term and long-term and the suitability of sources of finance
questions.q: A private limited company wants to raise a large amount of long-term finance to build a new factory without taking on debt. Which source fits best?
options: Hire purchase on a single vehicle
questions.explain: A new share issue raises a large amount of permanent, long-term finance without creating debt or interest. Overdrafts and trade credit are short-term, and hire purchase only finances a single asset.

questions.lo: The importance of cash and cash flow forecasts
questions.q: What is a cash flow forecast?
options: A list of the business's fixed assets
A calculation of the break-even output
A record of past profits made by the business
A prediction of the cash coming into and going out of a business over a future period
questions.explain: A cash flow forecast predicts future cash inflows and outflows, helping a business spot shortages in advance. It is not a record of past profit, an asset list or a break-even calculation.

questions.lo: Interpreting a cash flow forecast and the difference between cash and profit
questions.q: In a cash flow forecast, a month has an opening balance of 2,000 pounds, cash inflows of 8,000 pounds and cash outflows of 9,000 pounds. What is the closing balance?
questions.explain: Net cash flow = inflows - outflows = 8,000 - 9,000 = -1,000. Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow = 2,000 + (-1,000) = 1,000 pounds.

questions.lo: Interpreting a cash flow forecast and the difference between cash and profit
questions.q: Which statement best explains the difference between cash and profit?
options: Profit is always smaller than the cash balance
A profitable business can still run out of cash if money comes in later than it goes out
Only loss-making businesses ever have cash flow problems
Cash and profit are always exactly the same figure
questions.explain: Cash and profit are different: a profitable business can still face a cash shortage if it pays out cash before customers pay it, for example when selling on credit. Profit measures sales minus costs; cash measures money actually in the bank.

questions.q: Which of the following is a FIXED cost?
options: Raw materials used to make each product
Hourly wages that rise with output
questions.explain: Fixed costs do not change with the level of output; factory rent must be paid whether one unit or thousands are made. Raw materials, packaging per unit and output-based wages are variable costs that rise with production.

questions.q: A firm has fixed costs of 4,000 pounds and variable costs of 3 pounds per unit. If it makes 1,000 units, what are its TOTAL costs?
questions.explain: Total variable cost = 3 x 1,000 = 3,000. Total costs = fixed costs + total variable costs = 4,000 + 3,000 = 7,000 pounds.

questions.lo: Revenue, costs, profit and loss and the break-even level of output
questions.q: A business sells 500 units at 20 pounds each. Its total costs are 6,000 pounds. What is its profit?
questions.explain: Revenue = price x quantity = 20 x 500 = 10,000. Profit = revenue - total costs = 10,000 - 6,000 = 4,000 pounds.

questions.lo: Revenue, costs, profit and loss and the break-even level of output
questions.q: How is revenue (also called sales turnover) calculated?
options: Selling price per unit multiplied by the number of units sold
Selling price minus variable cost per unit
questions.explain: Revenue = selling price per unit x quantity sold. Fixed plus variable costs gives total costs, and selling price minus variable cost per unit gives the contribution per unit, not revenue.

questions.lo: Break-even output, margin of safety and break-even charts
questions.q: A product sells for 10 pounds and has a variable cost of 6 pounds per unit. Fixed costs are 8,000 pounds. What is the break-even level of output?
questions.explain: Contribution per unit = selling price - variable cost = 10 - 6 = 4 pounds. Break-even = fixed costs / contribution per unit = 8,000 / 4 = 2,000 units.

questions.lo: Break-even output, margin of safety and break-even charts
questions.q: A business breaks even at 2,000 units and is currently selling 2,500 units. What is its margin of safety?
questions.explain: Margin of safety = current output - break-even output = 2,500 - 2,000 = 500 units. This shows how far sales can fall before the business makes a loss.

questions.lo: Break-even output, margin of safety and break-even charts
questions.q: On a break-even chart, the break-even point is found where:
options: Total revenue is at its highest point
The variable cost line reaches zero
The fixed cost line meets the horizontal axis
The total revenue line crosses the total cost line
questions.explain: The break-even point is where the total revenue line crosses the total cost line, so revenue exactly equals costs and profit is zero. Left of it the business makes a loss; right of it, a profit.

questions.lo: Average rate of return on investment
questions.q: A machine costs 20,000 pounds and is expected to earn an average annual profit of 4,000 pounds. What is the average rate of return (ARR)?
questions.explain: ARR = (average annual profit / cost of investment) x 100 = (4,000 / 20,000) x 100 = 20%. A higher ARR means a more attractive investment.

questions.lo: Purpose and components of financial statements
questions.q: Which statement shows a business's assets and liabilities at a single point in time?
options: The statement of financial position (balance sheet)
questions.explain: The statement of financial position (balance sheet) is a snapshot of what the business owns (assets) and owes (liabilities) at one point in time. The income statement shows revenue, costs and profit over a period.

questions.lo: Gross profit margin and net profit margin
questions.q: A business has revenue of 50,000 pounds and gross profit of 20,000 pounds. What is its gross profit margin?
questions.explain: Gross profit margin = (gross profit / revenue) x 100 = (20,000 / 50,000) x 100 = 40%. It shows the percentage of sales revenue left after the cost of sales.

questions.lo: Gross profit margin and net profit margin
questions.q: A business has revenue of 80,000 pounds and net profit of 8,000 pounds. What is its net profit margin?
questions.explain: Net profit margin = (net profit / revenue) x 100 = (8,000 / 80,000) x 100 = 10%. Net profit margin is lower than gross profit margin because it also deducts overheads and other expenses.

questions.lo: Gross profit margin and net profit margin
questions.q: Why is net profit margin usually LOWER than gross profit margin?
options: Because net profit also deducts other expenses and overheads, not just the cost of sales
Because revenue is calculated differently for each
Because gross profit is always negative
Because net profit ignores the cost of sales
questions.explain: Gross profit only deducts the cost of sales, while net profit deducts the cost of sales AND all other expenses and overheads, so the net figure and its margin are smaller.
